headline: Code and Energy Compliance for Custom Home Builds in Los Angeles
articleBody: Custom home construction in Los Angeles County must comply with the **California Building Standards Code**, often called Title 24, which includes the California Residential Code and California Energy Code. The California Building Standards Commission adopts these codes statewide, and local jurisdictions like Los Angeles can enact additional amendments. LADBS publishes local code amendments that address regional risks such as seismic activity, wildfires, and hillside stability. The **California Energy Commission** explains that Title 24, Part 6 (Energy Code) sets performance requirements for building envelope insulation, windows, HVAC efficiency, lighting, and water heating. For custom homes, this often means higher R-value insulation, high-performance glazing, and efficient mechanical systems. California’s energy standards are some of the strictest in the U.S. and are updated on a three-year cycle, so design professionals typically use energy modeling (e.g., performance compliance approach) early in the design process to ensure the custom home meets or exceeds these requirements. The California Department of Housing and Community Development notes that the **California Green Building Standards Code (CALGreen)** adds mandatory measures for water efficiency, indoor air quality, and construction waste management. In high fire-risk areas of Los Angeles County, building officials enforce additional wildfire-resistant construction provisions adopted from the California Building Code and local ordinances, such as ignition-resistant exterior materials and ember-resistant vents. Seismic design provisions of the California Residential Code and amendments from the Structural Engineers Association of California influence foundation design, lateral bracing, and detailing. As a result, custom home builds in Los Angeles require coordination among architects, structural engineers, energy consultants, and contractors to integrate structural safety, energy efficiency, and environmental requirements into the plans submitted for permit review.
